name: Oksvik Fjordshell Anorak
description:
A pullover rain shell in a matte olive-grey fabric that sheds water like a second skin. The Fjordshell is cut long in the back, short in the front — a classic work-derived silhouette that keeps rain off your lower back without bunching when you sit. Single kangaroo chest pocket, drawstring hood that packs into its own collar, taped seams throughout. No insulation — this is a shell layer, worn over whatever you need underneath.

Oksvik is a mid-tier Scandinavian-heritage label now manufactured in the Milwaukee industrial district. Their stuff is functional and honest without being precious about it. The Fjordshell is what dock workers and infrastructure techs wear in the corridor's grey-season rains, and it's also what Tier 3 outdoor types buy because it actually works without advertising itself.
what_it_says: You care about staying dry more than you care about looking like you care about staying dry.
worn_by: anyone who walks to work in the rain
story_hooks: A particular batch of Fjordshells from the Milwaukee plant has a manufacturing defect — the DWR coating contains a trace compound that reacts with certain industrial runoff, staining the jacket a vivid rust-orange.
An infrastructure tech was last seen wearing an Oksvik Fjordshell before disappearing in a maintenance tunnel under the lakefront.
Oksvik's head of production has been quietly approached by a corponation looking to acquire the label — the workers on the floor have found out and aren't happy.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian pullover shell with purposeful asymmetry—cut longer at the back to protect the spine, shorter at the front for mobility when seated. Clean, unadorned silhouette with a modest technical presence. Reads as honest workwear rather than fashion statement.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed, ungendered cut through the shoulders and torso. Designed for layering—enough room for thermal base layers underneath without excess bulk. Hem sits mid-thigh in back, hip-length in front, creating subtle curved lines when worn.
physical_description.primary_material: Ballistic-grade synthetic blend, non-woven matte finish. Water-shedding treatment built into the fibers rather than surface-applied, so it survives repeated wear without degradation.
physical_description.texture: Smooth matte surface with visible taped seams running along shoulders, sides, and hood perimeter. Seams are functional landmarks—not hidden, but cleanly executed. Fabric has slight grip when dry, becomes slick when wet.
physical_description.color_scheme: Matte olive-grey—a desaturated sage-green-brown that absorbs light rather than reflecting it. No contrast trim, no logo noise. Single tone throughout.
physical_description.closures: Pullover entry with single-hand drawstring hood that cinches and packs into its own collar cavity. No buttons, zippers, or snaps—simplicity by design.
distinctive_features: Asymmetrical front-to-back hem length for dock/infrastructure work
Drawstring hood that retracts into collar pocket when not in use
Single kangaroo chest pocket—large enough for small tools or personal items
Taped seam construction throughout (shoulders, sides, hood perimeter, armholes)
Designed for 40+ years of manufacturing legacy—no trend markers
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 3 functional—honest mid-range pricing (≈120 Φ). Not cheap, not luxury. Built to last and perform.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by dock workers, infrastructure maintenance crews, field technicians, outdoor enthusiasts who value function over status. Also chosen by Tier 2 professionals who appreciate Scandinavian design philosophy. Signals competence and practicality rather than wealth or fashion awareness.
physical_description.condition_typical: Broken-in after a season of use. Water beading slightly diminishes but seam integrity remains. Possible patched areas on pocket edges from tool wear. No distressing—wear is quiet and authentic.

image_prompt: A matte olive-grey anorak photographed on a rain-slicked Milwaukee dock at dusk. Model is mid-40s, mixed heritage, wearing it over thermal base layers with weathered cargo pants. The anorak's asymmetrical hem is visible as model stands in 3/4 pose. Drawstring hood packed into collar. Moody industrial lighting with sodium vapor glow reflecting off wet concrete. Taped seams catch light subtly. Background shows shipping containers and grey Lake Michigan fog. No branding visible. Raw, honest workwear aesthetic. --ar 2:3 --v 6
